tasks.prompt: Order the leadership steps for approving the annual distribution operating plan for the whole system.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one annual operating plan covering all zones, storage, pumping and field programs.

cards.label: Compile last year performance, break, water quality and cost results for every program area
Set the plan priorities with zone supervisors, water quality and finance staff
Draft the operating plan with targets, owners and quarterly milestones for each program
Review the draft against Drinking Water Quality Management Standard commitments and regulatory duties
Present the plan to senior management for approval and record any changes directed
Issue the approved plan to all supervisors and track milestones at quarterly reviews

tasks.explanation: Priorities are built from measured results, not habit. The quality management check happens before approval so commitments are not approved that the operational plan cannot support, and quarterly tracking keeps an approved plan from becoming a shelf document.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for setting system wide performance targets for the distribution utility.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: annual targets for breaks, residuals, pressure, water loss, energy and customer service.

cards.label: Select the performance indicators that matter most to customers, regulators and asset health
Establish a verified baseline for each indicator from the last three years of records
Benchmark the baselines against comparable Ontario utilities and published guidance
Set a target and a stretch target for each indicator with the responsible supervisor
Assign the data source, reporting frequency and owner for every indicator
Review performance monthly and escalate any indicator trending off target for two periods

tasks.explanation: Targets need a trusted baseline before ambition is added. Benchmarking keeps targets honest, ownership and reporting frequency make them manageable, and the escalation rule acts on trends before a year end miss is locked in.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for preparing the annual distribution operations budget at utility scale.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: operating budget for labour, chemicals, energy, contractors, fleet and materials across all zones.

cards.label: Collect cost actuals and variance explanations from every cost centre for the past year
Forecast fixed costs, including labour, energy contracts and regulatory sampling, for the budget year
Build program bids for flushing, valve work, leak detection and repairs with unit quantities
Rank discretionary program bids by risk and service impact when funds are limited
Present the budget to senior management with the service consequences of each funding level
Load the approved budget into the financial system and issue spending limits to supervisors

tasks.explanation: Actuals and variances explain where money really went before new money is requested. Program bids are quantified so cuts can be ranked by risk, and management sees service consequences rather than discovering them after a cut.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for building a staffing and certification coverage plan for the distribution system.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: operator coverage for all shifts, zones and standby duties for the coming year.

cards.label: List every position, required certificate class and current holder from the staffing roster
Identify coverage gaps for vacations, training, standby and emergency call out
Confirm which operators are progressing toward the next certificate class and their timelines
Assign acting and backup coverage for the overall responsible operator and each supervisor role
Schedule training and examination preparation so coverage is not lost during study periods
Publish the coverage plan and review it whenever a resignation or long absence occurs

tasks.explanation: The roster and certificate record show the real gaps before schedules are promised. Backup coverage for senior roles is assigned in advance, and the plan is a living document that changes with staffing, not once a year.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for procuring a multi year contractor services agreement for distribution repairs.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: a three year agreement for emergency repairs, valve work and restoration support.

cards.label: Define the scope, response times and quality requirements from the last three years of work volumes
Set contractor qualification requirements, including licensing, safety record and insurance
Issue the competitive procurement with unit prices for the common repair tasks
Evaluate bids on price, response capability, past performance and safety, not price alone
Award the agreement and hold a start up meeting on standards, permits and reporting
Monitor contractor performance quarterly against response and quality measures and act on shortfalls

tasks.explanation: Scope and volumes come from real work history so unit prices are comparable. Evaluation weighs response and safety because the cheapest emergency contractor can be the most expensive failure, and quarterly monitoring enforces the agreement after award.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for reviewing and resetting customer service standards for distribution complaints.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: standards for pressure, discoloured water, leak and outage contacts across the system.

cards.label: Analyse complaint volumes, response times and repeat contacts by type and area for the past year
Compare current standards with the commitments published to customers
Identify the complaint types where field response, not call handling, drives dissatisfaction
Revise the standards with customer service and operations, setting realistic field response times
Train call centre and field staff on the revised standards and the escalation route
Report performance against the new standards to management every quarter

tasks.explanation: Complaint data separates a call handling problem from a field capacity problem before standards are rewritten. Joint revision keeps promises the field can keep, and quarterly reporting proves whether the new standards changed outcomes.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for implementing a work management system across distribution operations.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: system wide rollout replacing paper work orders for all distribution programs.

cards.label: Map the current work order, inspection and repair workflows with the supervisors who use them
Configure asset, work type and priority codes to match the mapped workflows
Load verified asset data and close or migrate open paper work before go live
Pilot the system in one zone and fix workflow and data problems found there
Train all crews and supervisors and set the date paper work orders stop being accepted
Audit work order completion and data quality monthly for the first year

tasks.explanation: Workflows are mapped with users first so the system fits the work instead of forcing work to fit software. A one zone pilot finds the data problems cheaply, and monthly audits protect data quality after the launch attention fades.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for strengthening records control for distribution operations.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: logbooks, sampling records, inspection reports and work records across all facilities.

cards.label: Inventory every record type, its retention requirement and where it is currently kept
Identify records that are incomplete, hard to retrieve or kept in duplicate conflicting versions
Issue a records standard naming the official copy, format and retention period for each type
Train supervisors to review and sign records on a set schedule rather than at audit time
Test retrieval by requesting sample records from each facility under time pressure
Report records readiness to management and close gaps before the next ministry inspection

tasks.explanation: An inventory exposes conflicting copies and retrieval failures that a policy alone never finds. Scheduled supervisory review replaces audit time panic, and a timed retrieval test proves the system works before an inspector tests it.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for the annual review of the health and safety program for distribution crews.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: confined space, excavation, traffic control, chlorine handling and driving risks for all crews.

cards.label: Compile incident, near miss and inspection results for distribution work over the past year
Review the hazard assessments for the highest risk tasks with crew representatives
Check training, permit and equipment inspection records for completeness
Update procedures and training plans for the gaps and new hazards identified
Present the review and the improvement actions to the joint health and safety committee
Track the improvement actions to closure and report progress at each committee meeting

tasks.explanation: Incident and near miss data show where the program failed in practice, and crew representatives keep hazard reviews grounded in field reality. Committee presentation and tracked actions turn an annual review into verified change.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for launching a continuous improvement program for distribution operations.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: a utility wide program inviting crew led improvements to quality, cost and safety.

cards.label: Collect improvement ideas and recurring frustrations from crews and supervisors across all zones
Screen the ideas for safety, regulatory and water quality impact before any trial
Select two or three low risk pilots with a named owner and a measurable outcome
Run the pilots for a set period and compare results with the baseline measures
Adopt the proven changes as standard procedure and update training and documents
Recognize the crews involved and publish the results and savings to all staff

tasks.explanation: Ideas come from the people who do the work, but screening protects safety and water quality before enthusiasm runs a trial. Measured pilots decide adoption, and publishing results keeps the next round of ideas coming.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for succession planning for senior distribution roles.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: succession for the overall responsible operator, utility manager and zone supervisor roles.

cards.label: Identify the senior roles where one departure would create a service or compliance risk
List the certification, experience and knowledge each role truly requires
Identify potential successors and assess their readiness honestly against the requirements
Build development assignments, acting opportunities and mentoring for each successor
Document the critical knowledge held by current role holders in procedures and records
Review readiness yearly and report the remaining single point risks to senior management

tasks.explanation: Risk roles are identified by consequence, not by seniority. Readiness is assessed honestly so development is real, acting opportunities test successors safely, and documenting knowledge reduces the risk while people develop.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for reviewing the system wide chlorine residual strategy.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: residual targets from plant entry points to the farthest extremities of every zone.

cards.label: Trend free chlorine residuals by zone, storage facility and extremity site for the past year
Identify where low residuals cluster by season, water age and storage operation
Compare entry point dosing, booster dosing and turnover practice against the findings
Set zone residual targets and the operational changes needed to hold them
Brief operators on the revised targets and the actions triggered at each threshold
Review residual compliance monthly and adjust the strategy at the seasonal change points

tasks.explanation: A year of trends separates seasonal patterns from local problems before targets move. Operational changes are matched to the cause in each zone, thresholds trigger defined actions, and seasonal reviews keep the strategy current.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for approving a nitrification action plan for system storage.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: chloramine affected storage and downstream areas showing nitrite and falling residuals.

cards.label: Confirm nitrification indicators, including nitrite, ammonia trends and residual loss, at the affected facilities
Rank the affected tanks and areas by severity and by population served
Select the response for each facility, such as deep cycling, breakpoint action or temporary free chlorine operation, with water quality staff
Set the sampling frequency and the exit criteria that show nitrification is controlled
Notify affected area operators and customer service of the plan and expected taste changes
Review indicator trends weekly until exit criteria are met, then restore normal operation gradually

tasks.explanation: Indicators confirm nitrification before disruptive responses are ordered. Responses are chosen per facility with exit criteria set in advance, and gradual restoration avoids declaring victory on one good sample.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for setting the dead end management strategy for the whole system.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: all dead end mains, including low use industrial spurs and seasonal services.

cards.label: Inventory every dead end main with its length, use pattern and residual history
Classify dead ends by water quality risk, from chronic low residual to no history of problems
Assign each class a control, such as scheduled flushing, an automatic flusher or main looping at renewal
Schedule the controls and record them in the work management system as recurring work
Sample the chronic sites after control to confirm residuals recover and hold
Review the inventory yearly and remove dead ends that looping or development has eliminated

tasks.explanation: Risk classification stops the common failure of flushing every dead end equally while the worst ones still fail. Controls are matched to class, recurring work makes them happen without reminders, and sampling proves the control works.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for designing the regulatory sampling program for a large system under Ontario Regulation 170/03.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: microbiological, chemical, lead and disinfection byproduct sampling for a system serving over 100,000 people.

cards.label: List every sampling duty by parameter, frequency, location type and regulatory deadline
Map sampling sites so every zone, storage facility and population area is represented as required
Build the annual calendar spreading samples evenly so no week carries an impossible load
Assign trained samplers and backup samplers for every scheduled week
Set the chain of custody, transport and laboratory arrangements and confirm holding times can be met
Audit the completed program quarterly against the regulation and correct any missed duty at once

tasks.explanation: Duties are listed from the regulation first, then sites and calendar are built to satisfy them without bunching. Backup samplers and confirmed holding times protect the program from ordinary absences, and quarterly audits catch a miss while it can still be explained and corrected.

tasks.prompt: Order the leadership steps after an adverse microbiological result is reported for the system.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one adverse result at a routine distribution sampling site, reported by the laboratory.

cards.label: Confirm the result details, site and sampling record with the laboratory and the sampler
Notify the local health unit and the ministry spill action centre as Ontario Regulation 170/03 requires
Direct resampling at the original site, upstream and downstream sites, with residual checks
Review recent work, breaks and pressure events near the site for a plausible cause
Hold the required notices and any advisory decision with the medical officer of health based on resample results
Complete the corrective action report and brief senior management on the outcome and lessons

tasks.explanation: Confirmation and statutory notification come first and in parallel with resampling, because the regulation sets the clock. Cause review runs alongside resampling, advisory decisions rest with the medical officer of health, and the corrective report closes the event formally.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for leading the community lead sampling program under the Ontario lead standard.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: plumbing and distribution lead sampling across residential areas of the system.

cards.label: Confirm the sampling periods, site counts and point of use requirements for the program year
Recruit and confirm volunteer premises spread across the older housing areas of the system
Train samplers on the required standing time, flushing and sample handling for each sample type
Track results against the lead standard as they arrive and flag any exceedance pattern by area
Notify participating households of their results with the required information and advice
Report the program results and any corrosion control referral to management and the health unit

tasks.explanation: Site recruitment is the long lead item, so it starts before the sampling window opens. Results are tracked by area as they arrive so a pattern is seen early, and households and the health unit receive results through the required channels.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for setting the disinfection byproduct monitoring strategy in distribution.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: trihalomethane and haloacetic acid sampling at the highest residence time sites.

cards.label: Identify the sampling sites with the longest water age in each zone from turnover and model data
Schedule sampling in the quarters and conditions the regulation requires, including the warmest period
Trend results by site over several years to separate seasonal peaks from a rising pattern
Where results trend upward, evaluate operational options such as turnover, flushing and entry quality referral
Implement the selected operational changes before the next high risk season
Report the trend and actions in the annual water quality summary for the system

tasks.explanation: Site selection follows water age because byproducts form with time. Multi year trending prevents overreacting to one warm summer, and operational changes are timed before the season that produces the highest results.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for approving a system wide unidirectional flushing program design.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: a multi year unidirectional flushing program covering every zone in sequence.

cards.label: Divide the system into flushing zones that can be isolated and flushed from clean source outward
Sequence the zones so the dirtiest and highest complaint areas are covered in the first year
Set the target flushing velocity and the valve operation sequence for each zone
Estimate water use, crew time and customer notice needs for the full program
Approve the program and schedule with management, including the water loss accounting treatment
Measure turbidity, residual and complaint results after each zone and adjust the next zone plan

tasks.explanation: Zone design comes before sequencing because unidirectional flushing only works from a clean source through an isolated area. Velocity and valve order are set per zone, and results from each zone improve the design of the next.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for evaluating a booster chlorination strategy for remote zones.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: a proposal to add booster disinfection at two storage facilities serving remote areas.

cards.label: Document the residual shortfall in the remote zones and the flushing and turnover effort now used
Assess the candidate facilities for space, power, chemical storage and operator access
Evaluate risks, including byproduct formation, chemical handling and overfeed protection
Pilot booster operation at one facility with enhanced residual and byproduct sampling
Compare pilot residuals, byproducts and operating cost with the current practice
Decide on system rollout, record the decision basis and set the operating targets if approved

tasks.explanation: The case starts from a documented shortfall, not from equipment enthusiasm. A single facility pilot with byproduct sampling tests the real tradeoff, and the rollout decision is recorded with its evidence.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for producing the annual water quality strategy report for senior management and council.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one annual report covering compliance, residuals, complaints and improvement programs.

cards.label: Compile compliance results, adverse events and corrective actions for the reporting year
Summarize residual, byproduct and lead program trends with the operational context
Report complaint patterns and how operational programs responded to them
State the water quality risks carried into the next year and the funded actions for each
Present the report to senior management and council with the overall responsible operator available for questions
Publish the report as required and file it with the system records

tasks.explanation: Compliance results lead because they are the legal record. Trends and complaints give the context numbers alone lack, risks are stated with their funded actions, and the overall responsible operator fronts the questions the report raises.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for leading the annual water loss audit for the whole system.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: a full water balance audit using system input, billed use and loss components.

cards.label: Confirm the audit boundary, period and the master meter data, and have master meters verified
Compile billed metered, billed unmetered and unbilled authorized volumes from billing records
Estimate apparent losses from metering inaccuracy, billing gaps and unauthorized use with stated methods
Calculate real losses as the balance remaining after authorized use and apparent losses
Grade the reliability of each audit component and list the data improvements needed
Present the audit, the loss levels and the reduction priorities to senior management

tasks.explanation: An audit built on unverified master meters is fiction, so meter verification comes first. Components are built in balance order, reliability grading is stated honestly, and management receives priorities, not just a percentage.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for rolling out district metered areas across the system as a loss strategy.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: staged creation of district metered areas covering the whole network over three years.

cards.label: Divide the network into candidate districts of manageable size using valves, geography and meter points
Rank districts by break history, night flow suspicion and metering readiness
Design the boundary, meters and data logging for the first districts and confirm boundary tightness
Commission the first districts and establish their baseline night flows
Use the first district results to refine the design and the rollout order for the rest
Report district loss levels quarterly and move the worst districts into active leak work

tasks.explanation: District design and ranking precede construction so the worst and most measurable areas go first. Boundary tightness is proven before baselines are trusted, and early districts teach the rollout rather than repeating the same mistakes system wide.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for setting up a minimum night flow analysis program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: routine night flow monitoring for all established district metered areas.

cards.label: Confirm each district boundary is tight and its inflow meter and logger are recording correctly
Establish the legitimate night use allowance for each district from customer and meter data
Set the night flow threshold for each district that triggers leak investigation
Review night flow data weekly and rank districts by flow above the legitimate allowance
Direct step testing or leak crews to the worst districts and record leaks found
Recalculate district night flow after repairs to confirm the saving and reset the baseline

tasks.explanation: Night flow only means something inside a tight, correctly metered boundary. Legitimate use is subtracted before leakage is claimed, thresholds trigger defined action, and post repair measurement proves the saving was real.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for prioritizing the annual leak detection survey program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: acoustic survey and correlation work allocated across zones for one year.

cards.label: Rank areas by break history, night flow results, soil and age data and previous survey findings
Allocate survey kilometres to the highest ranked areas within the crew and contractor capacity
Schedule surveys in the quieter traffic and lower noise periods that suit each area
Require found leaks to be marked, prioritized and handed to repair crews with a target date
Track leaks found per kilometre surveyed and water saved by area
Use the yield results to re rank areas for the next year program

tasks.explanation: Survey effort follows evidence of loss, not a rotation that treats all streets equally. Found leaks are worthless without a repair handover and date, and yield per kilometre is the measure that improves next year allocation.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for building an apparent loss reduction strategy focused on metering accuracy.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: large meter testing, small meter changeout analysis and billing data review.

cards.label: Analyse consumption and revenue by meter size, age and customer class from billing data
Test a sample of large meters and estimate the revenue and volume error they represent
Estimate small meter under registration from age based accuracy data and sample testing
Rank the fixes, such as large meter repair, targeted changeout and billing corrections, by payback
Implement the highest payback fixes and correct the billing processes that allowed the errors
Re audit apparent losses after one year and report the recovered volume and revenue

tasks.explanation: Billing data shows where to look before any meter is pulled. Large meters are tested first because a few large errors outweigh thousands of small ones, and process fixes stop the same errors returning after the hardware is fixed.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for approving pressure management as a system leakage reduction measure.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: a utility scale proposal to lower excess pressure in the highest pressure districts.

cards.label: Quantify excess pressure and leakage in the candidate districts from logger and night flow data
Confirm the minimum pressure needed for customers and fire flow in each district
Model the leakage and break frequency benefit expected at the proposed pressures
Price the pressure control works and the ongoing maintenance obligation
Approve a staged rollout starting with the district with the highest benefit and lowest risk
Measure night flow and break frequency after each stage against the pre project baseline

tasks.explanation: Excess pressure and leakage are quantified from field data before benefits are modelled. Fire flow and customer minimums set the floor, staging limits risk, and baselines fixed in advance let the claimed savings be audited.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for setting and tracking real loss reduction targets.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: a three year real loss target with annual milestones for the whole system.

cards.label: Establish the current real loss level from the validated annual water audit
Estimate the economic level of leakage where further reduction costs more than the water saved
Set the three year target between the current level and the economic level with annual milestones
Assign the programs, including pressure, survey and renewal, that must deliver each milestone
Track losses quarterly using production, night flow and repair data as leading indicators
Report progress and corrective actions to senior management at each year end

tasks.explanation: Targets are anchored to a validated audit and bounded by the economic level so the utility does not chase losses past the point of value. Programs are assigned to milestones, and leading indicators warn of a miss while the year can still be recovered.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for reporting non revenue water to council in a defensible form.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: an annual non revenue water report for a municipal council audience.

cards.label: Reconcile the audit volumes with finance and production records so all parties use the same numbers
Present non revenue water as component volumes, not only as a single percentage of supply
Explain the value of each component, including the cost of real losses and the revenue effect of apparent losses
State the funded reduction actions and the expected movement for the next year
Brief council members on why percentage alone misleads when production volumes change
File the report and the supporting audit with the utility records

tasks.explanation: Reconciliation comes first because council will hear different numbers if finance and operations are not aligned. Components and values replace the single percentage that hides whether the problem is leakage, metering or unbilled use.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for using main break data to find the drivers of system losses and cost.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: five years of break records analysed by material, age, pressure, soil and season.

cards.label: Clean the break records, removing duplicates and confirming location, material and cause fields
Analyse break rates by material, age band, diameter and pressure district
Compare break timing with pressure transients, temperature drops and construction activity
Identify the two or three drivers that explain most breaks and their operating areas
Direct the responses, such as pressure control, renewal priority or frost procedures, at those drivers
Repeat the analysis yearly and report whether the targeted drivers are improving

tasks.explanation: Dirty records produce confident nonsense, so cleaning comes first. Rate analysis by asset group separates age effects from pressure effects, and responses are aimed at proven drivers rather than the most recent memorable break.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for improving water audit data quality year over year.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: a data improvement plan following a first audit with low reliability grades.

cards.label: List every audit input with its current reliability grade and the reason for the grade
Rank the inputs by how much their uncertainty moves the final loss figures
Fund the fixes for the highest impact inputs, such as master meter testing and billing extracts
Assign each fix an owner and a completion date before the next audit
Re grade the inputs at the next audit and confirm the uncertainty actually fell
Report the audit confidence improvement alongside the loss results to management

tasks.explanation: Improvement money follows uncertainty impact, not ease. Master meter and billing data usually dominate the error, owners and dates make the plan real, and re grading proves the next audit deserves more trust than the last.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for reviewing pressure strategy across all zones of the system.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: a system wide review of zone pressures against service, leakage and energy goals.

cards.label: Compile pressure records, complaint history and leakage data for every zone
Compare each zone pressure with the level its highest and most distant customers require
Identify zones carrying excess pressure and zones at risk during peak and fire events
Decide the target pressure band for each zone with operations and water loss staff
Sequence the setpoint, valve and control changes needed to reach the target bands
Monitor pressures, complaints and night flows after the changes and report the outcome

tasks.explanation: Service need sets the floor for each zone before excess is declared. Leakage and complaint data show where pressure is costing money or service, and post change monitoring proves the new bands hold under real demand.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for developing a storage capacity strategy for system growth.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: a twenty year storage outlook covering growth areas, fire storage and equalization needs.

cards.label: Compile current usable storage by zone and the storage standard the utility designs to
Apply growth forecasts and peaking factors to project zone demands over the planning period
Calculate the storage shortfall by zone and the year each shortfall appears
Evaluate options for each shortfall, including new storage, zone changes and operational measures
Stage the preferred projects in the capital plan with their trigger years
Review the strategy whenever official growth forecasts or standards change

tasks.explanation: Current usable storage, not nameplate volume, is the honest starting point. Shortfalls are dated by zone so projects are triggered by need, and the strategy is revisited when forecasts change rather than defended as written.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for setting the system storage turnover and water age strategy.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: operating bands and cycling targets for all tanks and reservoirs.

cards.label: Calculate current turnover and estimated water age for every storage facility
Set a maximum target water age by season based on residual performance at extremities
Revise operating bands and fill schedules facility by facility to meet the age targets
Identify facilities that cannot meet targets by operation alone and flag them for mixing or capital review
Brief operators on the new bands and the residual triggers for extra cycling
Track age indicators and extremity residuals monthly and tighten bands where results require

tasks.explanation: Age is calculated before bands are moved so the size of the problem is known per facility. Most facilities respond to operation, the few that cannot are honestly flagged for capital, and monthly tracking keeps bands from drifting back.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for building the multi year storage inspection and rehabilitation strategy.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: inspection, coating and structural rehabilitation planning for all storage assets.

cards.label: Compile age, coating history and last inspection findings for every tank and reservoir
Rank facilities by condition risk and by the consequence of an unplanned outage
Schedule internal inspections so condition data stays current for the highest risk facilities
Convert inspection findings into rehabilitation projects with scope and staging
Place the projects in the capital plan in risk order with outage windows in low demand seasons
Update the strategy after each inspection cycle with the new condition evidence

tasks.explanation: Condition and consequence together set the order, because a poor coating in a sole source zone outranks a worse coating with backup storage. Inspection data feeds projects directly, and the strategy refreshes with evidence instead of aging on a shelf.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for setting the pressure reducing valve program strategy.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: inventory, criticality and maintenance strategy for all pressure reducing valve stations.

cards.label: Inventory every station with its area served, setting and maintenance history
Rank stations by consequence of failure, including customer count and pressure risk
Set inspection and overhaul intervals by criticality rather than one interval for all
Identify stations needing telemetry or pressure logging from their failure consequences
Fund the program in criticality order and schedule the first year work
Review station failures yearly and adjust intervals and the telemetry list from the evidence

tasks.explanation: One interval for all stations wastes effort on low risk sites and under serves critical ones. Consequence ranking drives intervals, telemetry and funding, and failure reviews keep the ranking honest.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for developing the fire flow capacity strategy for the system.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: system wide fire flow adequacy for existing areas and new development.

cards.label: Compile required fire flows by land use from the fire department and municipal standards
Test or model available fire flow across the system and map the deficient areas
Separate deficiencies caused by operations, such as valve position, from those caused by main capacity
Correct the operational deficiencies at once and verify them by retest
Place capacity deficiencies into the capital plan ranked by fire risk and development pressure
Report system fire flow status to the fire department and management annually

tasks.explanation: Required flows come from the fire service, not from engineering habit. Operational causes are fixed immediately because they are cheap and dangerous to leave, while capacity projects are ranked and reported so the residual risk is visible.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for setting booster station strategy for peak demand and fire events.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: firm capacity, standby power and control strategy for all booster stations.

cards.label: Confirm the firm capacity of each station with its largest pump out of service
Compare firm capacity with peak hour demand plus the fire flow the station must support
Identify stations short of firm capacity or without proven standby power
Set the upgrade and standby power priorities and place them in the capital plan
Prove each station under a witnessed full load and standby power test
Record the tested capacities in the emergency plan so response decisions use real numbers

tasks.explanation: Firm capacity with a pump out is the only capacity an emergency can count on. Gaps are priced into the capital plan, witnessed tests prove the paper numbers, and the emergency plan carries tested values rather than design claims.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for strengthening storage facility security and resilience.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: physical security, access control and contamination protection for all storage sites.

cards.label: Assess each facility for access points, hatch and vent security and intrusion detection
Rank vulnerabilities by the population served and the ease of unauthorized access
Install or repair locks, hatch alarms and vent screens in risk order
Set an access log and key control standard for staff and contractors
Include a security check in the routine facility inspection round
Review any intrusion or vandalism event and update the assessment from what it reveals

tasks.explanation: Assessment before hardware prevents spending on the most visible site instead of the most vulnerable one. Access control covers people as well as locks, and every real event updates the assessment because it tested the defences for free.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for approving seasonal pressure settings for the whole system.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: summer and winter pressure bands for zones with strong seasonal demand swings.

cards.label: Analyse seasonal demand, pressure and complaint patterns for the last two years
Propose the seasonal bands for each zone with the dates they would apply
Check the proposed bands against fire flow needs and the highest customers in each zone
Approve the bands and load the change dates into the operating calendar
Make the setpoint changes on the scheduled dates and verify critical point pressures
Review complaints and pressures after each season and adjust the bands for the next year

tasks.explanation: Two years of pattern data separate a real seasonal effect from one unusual summer. Fire flow and high customers bound the proposal, scheduled changes are verified in the field, and each season review improves the next.
